transcript.content:
I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-09-24 18:42 PDT (UTC-0700) (2026-09-25T01:42:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 3.014 degrees and its azimuth is 266.753 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 6.78 degrees and its azimuth is 103.997 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 96.97 percent illuminated, 159.91 degrees from the Sun, and 385592.3 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Based on the data you’ve provided, the short answer is: **It will be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to see the Moon with the naked eye at this specific moment.**

Here is the breakdown of why:

### 1. The "Daylight" Factor
The most significant hurdle is the Sun's position. At an altitude of **3.014 degrees**, the Sun is just barely skimming the horizon (it is about to set). Because the Sun is still above the horizon, the atmosphere is being flooded with direct sunlight. Even though the Moon is technically "up," the ambient light in the sky is far too bright for the human eye to distinguish a lunar disk against the blue of the daytime sky.

### 2. The Moon's Position
The Moon is at an altitude of **6.78 degrees**. This means it is very low in the sky, sitting just above the horizon. At this low angle, the Moon has to look through a much thicker layer of the Earth's atmosphere. This causes "atmospheric extinction," which makes celestial bodies appear dimmer and more distorted.

### 3. The Phase and Contrast
At **96.97% illumination**, the Moon is a Waxing Gibbous. While it is very bright, it is also very large and white. In bright daylight, a large white object low on the horizon tends to wash out into the glare of the atmosphere rather than standing out as a distinct shape.

### The Verdict
Because the Sun is still above the horizon, you are essentially trying to see a flashlight (the Moon) while someone is shining a stadium floodlight (the Sun) right next to it. 

**Your best chance:**
If you want to see it, you should wait about **15 to 20 minutes**. Once the Sun drops below the horizon (civil twilight begins), the sky will begin to darken rapidly. Because the Moon is so close to full and relatively high in its cycle, it will "pop" out against the deepening blue of the twilight sky much more clearly than it will right now while the Sun is still visible.

**Summary:** Right now, you likely won't see it. In 20 minutes, you'll have a much better chance!
